segments: Your alarm screams in your ear at 10 a.m., rudely disrupting a dream about your childhood golden retriever.  Groaning, you sit up and snatch your phone from the nightstand, pushing your knotted hair away from your face.  The alarm title flashes.
One month. Thirty days since Adam broke your heart and ran away with the pieces. Fantastic.
You snooze the alarm.
Turning away, you face-plant in a pile of crumpled tissues, damp with tears and snot from last night’s one-woman pity party.
You freeze. Something just touched your leg.
You throw the comforter back.

Peering across the bed, you eye Adam’s stuffed bear.  How did your ex’s gift end up in your bed again? You recall stashing it in your closet last night.  This relationship withdrawal is getting out of control.
Your gaze lands on the piano.  You pushed it to the dark corner of the room days after the breakup, trying to hide the sick reminder of the happy days when you and Adam played this piano together.
You glance back at your phone, biting your lip.
This calls for Tinder.
You tap on the dating app’s icon and it opens to a smirking guy with a butt chin.
You swipe right to like him.
He has John Travolta’s chin, so he must be at least half as entertaining.  It’s a match.
Twenty seconds later, a message pops up in your inbox.  “You’re an Avenger and you have to choose a side. Are you Team Captain America or Team Iron Man?”  Marvel superheroes? Interesting opener.
You type, “Team Captain America.”
“Good answer. Seems like we are a match indeed.  I’ll be at the Game Zone arcade in 30 minutes. Hope to see you there.”  You sigh, hugging your phone to your chest.  It’s a date.
Wait a minute. Panic sets in as you realize that you haven’t been on a first date in over two years.
You need to call your best friend.  You press 1 on speed-dial.
Lex picks up on the first ring. “Happy monthiversary!”  Ugh...this is not what you want to hear!  That this is the 30th day since your breakup does not make you feel any better. How frustrating!
“I don't like this conversation starter!”
A soft click. Lex hangs up, but you know her too well to expect the conversation to end there.  Within seconds, your phone is ringing again.

Rolling your eyes, you answer. “Yes?”  Lex scoffs. You can picture her frowning through the phone.  “Sorry to interrupt your busy schedule of sobbing and shoving junk food in your face.”  You stroke the can of Pringles on your nightstand. “Chips are friends. Not food.”  “You’re the worst, and I’m the best. I’m taking you out. Now.”  A car engine starts in the background. “Be over in five.”
You hang up, crawling back under your covers and pulling the sheet over your head.  Five minutes later, you hear a dull thud across the room.
You sit up.
Another thud.  You throw the covers to the side, moving to the window to investigate.  A yellow blur flies through the air, smacking against the glass.
You peer down at the top of Lex’s blonde head, which is covered in her trademark blue and pink highlights.  Poised to throw another yellow square at your window, she waves.

You slide your feet into a pair of fuzzy slippers and squint at the mirror by the door.  Your My Little Pony shirt from middle school isn’t the most flattering.  Neither is your nest of uncombed hair or growing unibrow.
You should spice up the outfit.
Throwing on a pair of sunglasses, you glance back at the mirror.  Now you’re fully dressed.

You run down two flights of stairs and push open the front door.  You approach Lex, who is lounging on the hood of her car.  You point at your building. “That was vandalism.”  Lex shrugs. “I had a feeling you weren’t going to buzz me in.”

You scoop up a yellow packet from the grass. “You were throwing Peanut M&M’s at my window?”  Lex tears open a packet and pops a few in her mouth. “Have a few. Consider it an incentive to avoid a 100-foot radius of he-who-shall-not-be-named.”  Adam is deathly allergic to peanuts, so your diet has been practically Peanut M&M-free since you started dating.
It’s about time you tried one again.
Staring at the cartoon M&M characters, you can’t curb your curiosity.  You open the packet, place an M&M on your tongue and let it melt.  Two years is a long time.  You forgot how great they tasted.

Lex stands, squinting at the sun. “Come on, Emily. Let’s get you presentable.”  With Lex behind, you trudge back up the stairs to your apartment.  Within moments, Lex’s pierced nose is buried in your closet.  She extracts two dresses and throws them at you, raising an eyebrow.  You rub the skirt fabrics between your fingertips, exhaling.
What to wear to re-enter civilization?  The white dress might stain easily, but the red dress reminds you of Adam.
You pull the red dress over your head.
As you stare at the mirror, the blood drains from your face.

You haven’t worn something like this for so long, and you don’t remember anything about how to date.  Hopefully you won’t be a klutz today, but who knows.  Your brain is anywhere but the present.  Lex drops you off at the arcade 20 minutes later, tossing a tube of pepper spray out the window as she drives away.  You narrowly catch it and slip it into your purse, then turn and head inside.

When you enter, you realize the entire arcade is under black light, meaning your dress makes you look like a massive glowstick.  You survey the room, which is a mess of blinking screens, basketball hoops, and ski ball machines. It smells like sweat.

You squint as you recognize your date.  He’s wearing a jean jacket with glowing patches, eyes trained on his phone.  You approach him and clear your throat, suddenly realizing you don’t remember his name.  Your phone is snugly buried in your purse, so it would be hard to subtly check.  He turns to you and grins. “Hey, you. Right on time.”  He slips his phone into his shirt pocket. “Can I get you something to drink?”
"Yes, please."

You follow him to the counter, careful not to lean your dress against the various soda stains and loose kernels of popcorn.  Your date already has a drink in his hand, so he glances at you for your selection.
You select the red fruit punch.
It would be boring to just order a water when someone else is paying.
You thank Tinder Guy, accept the cup and take a sip. You taste a hint of contamination with some sweet soda.

The flavor reminds you of the Saturdays you and Adam spent volunteering at the local daycare center near your campus, which sends another wave of sadness through your body.  You wonder what Adam’s doing right now.  He’s probably at the daycare.  You wonder if he still volunteers there.
Tinder Guy holds up a string of blue tickets, which snaps you out of your thoughts. “Which game first?”
You nod at the basketball hoop.
You have your eye on the penguin behind the front counter.  It’s worth something like 50 tickets, but Adam hates penguins.

“That stuffed penguin is looking pretty cute.” It’s about time you stopped sleeping with the stuffed bear Adam gave you last Christmas.  At this point, it’s just sad.  It can’t be ethical to bury a stuffed animal in snot-filled tissues every night.
Tinder Guy digs around in his pocket and produces a handful of quarters, holding one up. “Let’s spice this game up. You call the flip.”
"Heads.”
He throws the coin in the air. “Heads, you take a spin at it. Tails, I show off my mastery.”  It lands on the opposite of your bet.
Tinder Guy smiles and passes his drink to you.  You accept it in your free hand.

He sticks out his tongue in concentration, aiming carefully.  He misses. Tinder Guy runs a hand through his hair, then cracks his knuckles in preparation. He aims again, and this time he succeeds. He cheers, throwing his arms up as he takes a step back towards you. The motion knocks the cups out of your grip. His Dr. Pepper splashes all over your dress.  He winces, scratching his neck. “Dude, sorry about that. Bad luck.”

He collects the tickets from the machine and points at the penguin. “Mind if I keep that? My mom loves penguins.” Still in shock, you glower at him.  He glances around. “There’s no bathroom here, but there’s one at Firefly Café down the street. I could walk you there?”
“It’s the least you could do.”

He ruined your dress. Bare minimum, he buys you a coffee, then helps you salvage the mess.  No point in cleaning the thing before drinking another spill hazard around him.  As the café appears around the corner, Tinder Guy mutters an excuse about spending the last bit of his cash at the arcade.  A new level of cheap. He wants you to buy him a coffee in exchange for the soda you’re now wearing.  Best date ever.

Firefly Café is the go-to coffee spot near your college campus, and as you walk in, all five senses are entangled in its hazy ambiance.  The strong smells of coffee and chocolate mingle in the air.  Heat blasts from air vents framing the café’s tiled walls, which are covered in portraits of coffee beans and animated customers.  The window seats are occupied by students with furrowed brows, headphones blasting as they hunch over textbooks.

Nothing has changed in your month-long boycott of the café.  It was easier to forget Adam if you didn’t have to sip coffee in the same shop where you first met.  Head buried in your purse, you take a couple of steps toward the coffee bar.

A loud voice sounds from your right. “Excuse me.”  You look up to see a vaguely familiar face.  You recognize the guy from your Intro to Mass Communication class.  He gestures at a girl sitting in a booth. “Would you mind taking a photo for us?”  Your brain goes into panic mode. You’re terrible at taking photos.
You hold out your palm.

He thrusts his phone into your hand. “Thank you so much.”  He lowers his voice. “Instead of taking a photo, can you hit the record button?”  Easy enough. You nod, sliding to video mode and holding the screen up.  He pulls his drawstring bag off his shoulder and retrieves a ukulele, dropping to a knee in front of the girl.  Her eyes widen, hand covering her mouth.  All eyes in the cafe turn to the couple.  Strumming the opening to “Marry Me” by Train, the guy sings until he gets to the end of the chorus.  At that point, the girl nods and throws her arms around his neck.  Looks like your break-up’s monthiversary will be someone else’s anniversary.

The door jingles. You turn and see it inch open and shut as a little pug nudges it with its face.  Trapped outside, it looks up at you with sad eyes.  You glance at the couple and back at the pug.  You’re still recording. Should you let the dog in and risk messing up the video?
You decide against it.

Another customer enters. As the door opens, the dog shuffles inside and runs to the guy with the ukulele.  He reaches down and retrieves a ring from the pug’s collar, then slides it onto his new fiancé’s finger.  The coffee shop crowd cheers and claps.  After a few more seconds, you end the recording.  The guy returns and retrieves his phone, grinning.  You plaster a smile on your face. “Congratulations.”  He’s glowing, face all flushed. “Thank you.”
You continue toward the counter, head down.  Their lives are forever changed, and you’re stuck in post break-up limbo.  Nothing is changing. Nothing is new.

You look up to order. Correction: the hot barista? That’s new.  All tattooed muscles and beanie, the guy behind the counter sticks his pen behind his ear as he enters numbers into the register. As you approach, your eyes linger on his nametag.  Ryan. Of course, his name is Ryan.  One more addition to the long list of attractive Ryan’s – Ryan Gosling, Ryan Reynolds, Ryan Seacrest.
You continue to observe.

The hot barista switches his focus to organizing sugar packets. Hello?  Peripheral vision, anyone?  After a very long minute, you clear your throat.  He glances up, his dark eyes and long lashes meeting your gaze. Silence.

Oh, right. You’re supposed to order. “Two daily specials, please.”  Ryan chews on a toothpick, squinting at you.  You tilt your head. “What?”  He shrugs. “You don’t strike me as a ‘daily special’ customer.” Your eyes dart to the menu, which is filled with tiny print and dozens of flavor combinations.
“What does a ‘daily special’ customer look like?”
The toothpick tilts as the corners of Ryan’s mouth lift. “Two daily specials, coming up.” He rings up the order.

You open your wallet. “If I bribe you, is there any chance you’ll spit in one of the coffees?”  Ryan glances at Tinder Guy, who is currently drooling at a girl in an Avengers shirt a few tables down from him.  What a catch. Ryan scoffs. “For that guy over there? I’d do it for free.”  There’s no universe where Ryan could be any cooler.  You pass him a $5 bill. He hands you an order number and turns to mix the drinks.

When you return to the table, Tinder Guy has his phone beneath the table.  You glance at it from above and spot the familiar Tinder interface.  No way. He’s swiping through other girls in the middle of a date with you.  You sit, clenching your jaw.  You stare at the side of his head for a minute before he glances up.  He ignores the irritated look on your face.  That, or he has zero social awareness.

He sighs. “Hey, my friend just had an emergency and needs to meet me here in a minute. Hate to do this, but is there any way we could end early?”  His eyes shift to the door.  You follow his eyes to a girl who stands outside.  She waves through the window and tilts her head, confirming his identity.  She clearly doesn’t know him well.  He can’t be serious. He expects you to buy him a free coffee and then get out of this nightmare by exchanging girls?
Ryan appears with the two coffees.  You stand and take one from his tray.
You pour it on his shirt.

Tinder Guy is lucky the coffees here are never more than lukewarm.  Tinder Guy jumps to his feet, screeching. “What was that for?”  Your eyes widen. “What wasn’t it for? My dress, your mom’s penguin, and the girl outside the door."  His face confirms your read of the situation.  In your peripheral vision, Ryan stifles a smile.  Tinder Guy shakes his head, picking up the penguin and tucking it under his arm. “I’m out of here.” He glances at Ryan. “See you tonight, man.”  He stalks off, the bell jingling as he makes his grand exit.

Ryan whistles. “I’m surprised that doesn’t happen more often.”  He chuckles. “I wouldn’t recommend drinking the one in my hand. I’ll make you a fresh cup, on the house.”  He starts toward the bar, then glances over his shoulder. “I spit in this one.”  You almost wish you had let Tinder Guy drink it
You watch Ryan work.

You don’t know much about making coffee, but you’re pretty sure he has perfect technique.  He swings by with a full cup and sets it down in front of you.  You open your mouth to say something cute or stupid, but an important-looking lady calls him to the back room.

You hear faint arguing from the back room.  Ryan emerges, pulling his apron off his head and placing it on a barstool.  Face red, he scoops up a set of keys from behind the counter and storms out of the café.  You wonder what happened.
His boss takes his position at the counter, her face a matching shade of red.
You walk over to investigate.

“Hi. Do you know where Ryan went? I was hoping to order a scone.”  She shakes her head. “Ryan no longer works here, but I can grab you one.” She turns to the bakery display.  You furrow your brow. “That’s okay, thanks. I’m not hungry anymore.”
You run after Ryan.
He got a head start, but there’s a chance he’s still around.

You don’t really know him, but you want to make sure he’s okay.  He stands by a parked car.  “Hey!” You catch up to him. “Everything okay?”  Ryan stares at the ground. “I just got fired, so no.”  You gape. “I’m so sorry.”  He kicks a pebble lightly. “It happens. Served one too many free coffees in my first week. Had a strict supervisor on this shift. I should’ve been more discreet.”  He sits in the driver’s seat. “Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to go.”
You feel terrible. He got fired because of your coffee. You messed up pretty bad.  Seeing his car head off, you know there’s only one place you can go, and you have the walk memorized.

You disrupt a 30-person Starbucks line that snakes out the shop door.  As you pass mannequins in flowy skirts inside a store window, you almost step on a squirrel trying to bury an acorn in a sidewalk crack. Lex lives in a three-story sorority house a few blocks from your apartment.  Towering Greek letters loom over the entrance.  You duck under strands of ivy as you knock on the door.

To your relief, Lex answers.  Her eyes flit across your face and she welcomes you in, reading the situation wordlessly.  You enter her room, which is filled with plants and succulents of various sizes.  A bouquet of wildflowers she collected from her last hike fills a clear vase on her desk.  She pulls out her chair and pats the back, bending down to retrieve her cosmetics collection from a bottom drawer.

You sit, pulling your hair into a ponytail.  Lex’s solution to heartache? Five layers of makeup, a tight dress and a frat party.  In the next hour, Lex applies thirty products you’ve never heard of while issuing directions in a pattern of tilting your head, relaxing your forehead, and closing your eyes.  Finally, Lex makes a fish face and you mimic her.  She brushes a final swipe of makeup onto your cheeks and grins, stepping back.  You smile in the mirror. “I have cheekbones.”  She laughs, hugging you from behind. “I know. I’m a miracle-worker.”  She touches up her own lip gloss. “You’re going to be okay. Okay? I’m taking you to a house full of fraternity snobs.

You’ll forget all about terrible Tinder dates and cute guys getting fired.”  Lex tosses a clean dress at you, grabs a clutch and starts out the door.  You whimper, dabbing at your eyes with a tissue. “Too soon.”
As soon as you enter the party, you note the classic sticky floor, active game of beer pong and clusters of sweaty dancers.  Lex screams, throwing her arm around a group of her sorority sisters.

One girl breaks away from the cluster and skips over to you.  You’ve seen her at one or two parties.  She points at you, grinning. “You’re Adam’s girlfriend.”  Your throat catches. “Ex.”  “Oh.” Her eyes twinkle. “I know a secret.” She leans closer.  The smell of beer shoots up your nose. “Do you want to know?”
Tell me.
Her gaze darts across the room. “Lex never thought you were good together.”  She giggles. “I shouldn’t have said that.”  She waves at a friend and disappears into the crowd.

You search for Lex, who is already engrossed in a game of Charades in the next room.  Crossing your arms, you melt into the background and peer over the shoulder of an onlooker.  A frat guy holds up a dry erase marker. “Alright, I’m looking for a volunteer brave enough to take on Lex, the Master of Charades herself.”
You start to turn away.

He points at you, gesturing with the marker. “Who better than Lex’s best friend? Come on up.”  The crowd parts and you step up to the deck of cards.  Selecting one, you scoff.  Your prompt is a snake. The irony.  You draw a messy squiggle with a forked tongue on the wall they’ve sacrificed for the game.  Lex snaps her fingers. “Snake.”  You confirm and the crowd cheers with excessive enthusiasm.  “Yes, she’s wonderful.”

You tug at Lex’s arm, pulling her back to the lobby.  Lex pokes your nose. “What’s up?”  You bite your lip, trying to piece together a coherent string of words. “Did you approve of my relationship with Adam?”  Lex coughs, teasing her hair. “What kind of question is that?”  Your cheeks are hot. “Did you?”  She clears her throat. “No.”  A pause. “I thought you deserved better.”

Another pause. “You know who I do like for you?”  She scans the room and points at the balcony, winking at you.  You smile, giving her a hug before you turn to the balcony and spot a familiar head of messy curls.  Ryan from Firefly Café. He sports a polo shirt with a popped collar, leaning against the railing with a drink in his hand.
Wait...is that the Tinder Guy in the door's reflection?  Why is he here?  The memory of the horrid time you spent with him earlier comes back to you. Ugh!
That's your cue to hide.

You immerse yourself in Lex’s shroud of sorority sisters.  After the fiftieth selfie, you need to sit down.  You feel the start of a headache pounding at your skull and plop down on the couch.  Red solo cups crunch beneath your feet.  The couch sags beneath your weight, squeaking.  You try to melt into the music, but just as you feel your stress level going down, Tinder Guy approaches.  He’s clearly out of it.
You cross your arms. “Hey.”  He narrows his eyes at you. “Are you the person who poured coffee on me earlier?”  You raise an eyebrow.  “Are you the person who spilled soda on me earlier?”

Ryan appears suddenly, placing a hand on Tinder Guy’s shoulder. “The other team’s winning. You should get back to your game.” Tinder Guy blinks, swearing under his breath.  Reluctantly, he picks up a ping pong ball and returns to the game.
Ryan sits next to you.  You scramble for a way to break the ice.  He keeps his eyes trained on Tinder Guy, taking a sip from his cup.

You notice the tattoo on his wrist for the first time.  You recognize the symbol from an article you did on the school’s archeological museum. “Viking Compass. Solid pick. Guidance through the unknown.”  Ryan raises an eyebrow. “Impressive. Not exactly a dinner table fact. Archeology major?”  “Journalism. It’s my job to know the random facts.”

From there, it’s like time pauses to listen to your conversation.  You learn about Ryan’s kid sister and her adventures with braces, Ryan’s dream home in the Arizona desert, his platinum molar from sledding into his elementary school seesaw when he was seven.  In three hours, he transforms from a hot barista into the guy who’s afraid of needles but loves symbolism, thinks the weathermen are TV’s branch of the Illuminati, and dimples at your worst jokes.  For three hours, you remember what it feels like to have temporary abs from laughter.
Then, Lex lies on your lap and passes out, disrupting the flow of the conversation.
You should stay for a bit.
Right on cue, Lex starts to gag like she’s going to puke.  It only lasts a moment before she falls back to sleep, but you know that you can’t let her stay here any longer.  You need to get her home.
“I understand. Need help?”  You shrug. “That would be great, thank you.”

After your experiences with Adam, it’s strange for a guy to be so proactive about helping.  At some point in the relationship, he stopped trying to be a gentleman.  Maybe there was more wrong there than you had thought.

As you start toward the door, Tinder Guy steps in front of you.  He reeks of alcohol. “You shouldn’t leave a guy's house without apologizing for ruining his shirt.”  He wipes at an eye, and you can’t tell if he’s ready to cry or to fall asleep. “It was my favorite Tinder date shirt.”  Ryan steps between you, making himself a physical barrier.  “Go. I’ve got him," he says, patting Tinder Guy on the back and steering him away.
Tense, you usher Lex into her car.

You glance back at the house for a long moment, taking in the pulsing colors spilling out from the windows.  Even from the street, you can feel the beat of the music drumming inside your chest.  You want to always remember how it felt to be standing outside of the frat house with the sticky floor, nose threatening to run, a million possible memories waiting in the arms of the guy right inside the door.  As soon as your nose actually starts to run, you duck into the driver's side and start the engine.

You didn’t get a chance to exchange contact info, but his face is burned into your memory.  You have a feeling you’ll run into him again. It’s a small enough campus.  When you get back to your building, you help Lex into the elevator and lay her down on your living room couch.

Throwing a blanket over her, you enter your bedroom and shut the door.  You slide open your closet.  Standing on your tiptoes, you retrieve a box from the top shelf.  You set it down on your bed and peer inside.  Movie ticket stubs, anniversary cards, souvenirs from your trips to New York, and band tees from various stadium tours stare back at you.  Time is strange, isn’t it?  Two years of happiness reduced to a pile of paper and polyester in a duct-taped box.

You glance at the clock. Eleven fifty-five.  Five minutes until your cheat day is over and you really need to move on with your life.  You sit cross-legged on your fluffy rug, hugging the box to your chest.  Relationships are beautiful.  They’re starry nights and jealous tears.  They’re intertwined hands and heads on shoulders at movie theaters, blocking the vision of the annoying kid kicking the back of your seat.  They’re messy buns and pizza stains on Friday nights spent watching Harry Potter movie marathons.  And for each beautiful memory, each precious moment, you trade a little piece of yourself.  You can’t unsee the stars, un-cry the tears, forget how good it felt to hold onto someone stable and strong and vulnerable.  And no matter how hard you squeeze your eyes shut and click your heels together, you’ll never be the same exact person you were a relationship ago.

At the end of the day, you’re left with a box of memories and a choice:  you either let go of that part of you that isn’t yours anymore, or you hold onto the sadness and close your heart to a new shot at happiness.  The clock reads eleven fifty-nine.  You brush a handful of stray tears from your wet cheek with the back of your hand and stand.
You throw the box away.
That's that. You blink hard, unsure what to do next.

Your eyes pan the room, landing on a relic of the past.  You feel inexplicably drawn to it.  For the first time in a month, you sit down on your piano bench and turn on your keyboard.  You slide your headphones over your ears.  Your fingers take their familiar positions on the black and white keys, making an indent in the thin layer of dust that accumulated in the past few weeks.

Adam loved this piano. You used to spend afternoons playing together.  Your heart would flutter every time his hand brushed yours, even two years into the relationship.  You thought destiny was the reason your butterflies never went away until the butterflies stayed and Adam left.
You close your eyes, letting the music flow from your fingertips.  It empties your shaking hands and broken heart, filling them with something new.  Welcome to the first day of the rest of your life.
The End.
